newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: E. Timor leader Horta to address U.N. rights forum.
newsitem.headline: E. Timor leader Horta to address U.N. rights forum.

text.p: East Timorese independence leader Jose Ramos Horta, co-winner of the 1996 Nobel peace prize, will address the U.N. Commission on Human Rights on Thursday, a U.N. spokeswoman said on Tuesday.
But diplomats said Asia's representative, backed by the African group in a closed-door meeting, argued Horta could only address the 53-member forum from the floor -- not the podium.

Horta, a long-time campaigner for self-determination on the disputed island, could embarrass Indonesia by urging the Commission to adopt a strongly worded resolution criticising Jakarta and calling for an end to alleged abuses in East Timor.
It was possible that Horta would address the 2,000 delegates on behalf of the International Service for Human Rights, although negotiations continued and no decision had been reached, diplomats said.
"We are still pushing for him to address the Commission from the podium. There is some resistance," a spokeswoman from the Geneva-based non-governmental organisation told Reuters.
"We would like for him to speak not on behalf of our organisation, but as a Nobel Peace Prize laureate. But if it has to be, yes we will (have him speak on our behalf)," she added.

Horta's speech would be in open session in either case. Rigoberta Menchu, a Guatemala-born Maya Indian, and former Archbishop Desmond Tutu of South Africa are among the previous Nobel Peace prize laureates to address the body from the podium.
The U.N.'s main human rights body, now in the second week of its annual six-week session in Geneva, last April expressed its "deep concern" over reported violations of rights in East Timor.
Indonesia invaded East Timor in 1975 after Portugal withdrew form its former colony, which Indonesia annexed the next year.

The international community does not recognise the annexation and talks under U.N. auspices between the foreign ministers of Portugal and Indonesia, aimed at finding an internationally-acceptable solution, have dragged on since 1983.
The U.N. special envoy for East Timor, Jamsheed Marker, is due in Indonesia next week on a familiarisation trip, according to diplomats in New York.
